channel.title: Post-Trained
channel.description: A 20-episode audio course on language models, reinforcement learning and post-training: from n-grams and the Transformer to PPO, DPO, GRPO, reasoning models, coding agents, reward hacking and RL infrastructure. Two hosts, Maya and Sam.
channel.itunes:author: Post-Trained

item.title: 1. Before the Transformer
item.itunes:title: Before the Transformer
item.description: A language model factorizes sequence probability by the chain rule; sequence log-prob is the sum of token log-probs — the same object policy gradients act on later. Maximum likelihood minimizes forward KL (mass-covering, hedging); RL with a KL penalty uses reverse KL (mode-seeking) — one reason post-trained models are sharper and less diverse. Cross-entropy = entropy + KL; perplexity = exp(mean NLL per token). Compare across tokenizers only via bits per byte; post-training can raise web-text perplexity while making the model more useful. n-grams failed from sparsity (smoothing: Good-Turing, Katz, Kneser-Ney continuation counts); neural LMs generalize via learned embeddings, but the full softmax was the compute bottleneck for a decade.

item.title: 2. Attention Is All You Need
item.itunes:title: Attention Is All You Need
item.description: Scaled dot-product attention: softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V. The sqrt(d_k) keeps score variance near 1 so softmax doesn't saturate. Multi-head = many narrow heads for about the cost of one wide head; heads specialize (induction heads). Causal masking lets one forward pass train all positions in parallel (teacher forcing, parallelized). Generation remains sequential with a KV cache — cheap scoring vs. expensive generation is the core economics of RL for LLMs. Positions: sinusoidal -> learned absolute -> relative (Shaw, T5, ALiBi) -> RoPE. Long context via position interpolation, NTK-aware base scaling, YaRN, or large RoPE base; check rollouts stay within the model's comfortable context. Residual stream as a shared bus; pre-norm (GPT-2 onward) trains stably vs. post-norm needing warmup; RMSNorm drops mean-centering. QK-norm, soft-capping, and z-loss all fight logit growth.

item.title: 3. Scale
item.itunes:title: Scale
item.description: Decoder-only generative pretraining won because a generative model can do any task as text, and a generative model is a policy that RL can optimize. Loss follows power laws in parameters, data and compute. Training FLOPs are about 6 times N times D; inference is about 2 times N per token. Always do this arithmetic and compare to MFU. Chinchilla: scale parameters and tokens roughly equally, about 20 tokens per parameter. Kaplan's different answer traced largely to learning-rate schedules not matched to run length. Product models deliberately overtrain because inference cost dominates. Repeating data up to about 4 epochs is nearly as good as fresh data; beyond that, returns fall off.

item.title: 4. The Language Model as a Policy
item.itunes:title: The Language Model as a Policy
item.description: Models see token IDs. Byte-level BPE learns merges greedily from 256 byte symbols, so nothing is out of vocabulary. Tokenization is many-to-one: in RL, keep the sampler's exact token IDs and never decode and re-tokenize. Build agent transcripts incrementally with a policy-token mask. Tokenizer quirks: leading-space tokens, inconsistent number chunking, glitch tokens, prompt-boundary effects, special tokens that must not be injectable from user text. Log-softmax equals logit minus log-sum-exp, computed with max subtraction and in fp32. Logits at position t score the token at t plus one. The logits tensor is huge, so compute log-probs in chunks or with fused kernels. Sampling: greedy and beam search degenerate for open-ended text; temperature divides logits; top-k, top-p, min-p truncate. In RL the sampler must equal the policy: sample at temperature 1 without truncation or penalties, or account for them consistently.

item.title: 5. RL Fundamentals I
item.itunes:title: RL Fundamentals I
item.description: An MDP is states, actions, transitions, rewards, discount. An LLM is a policy in a token-level MDP with deterministic transitions and usually one terminal reward, with gamma set to 1. The whole-response view is a contextual bandit. V is the value of a state, Q the value of a state-action pair, and the advantage A equals Q minus V. Bellman equations write values recursively. Dynamic programming solves them when the model is known, which never applies to LLMs. Exploration: you only learn from what you sample. For LLMs that means policy entropy and multiple samples per prompt. Prompts that always pass or always fail give no signal once you use a baseline. Policy gradient theorem via the log-derivative trick: the gradient of expected reward equals the expected sum of grad log pi times return. Dynamics drop out, so rewards can be black boxes like unit tests and graders. Discrete tokens and non-differentiable rewards rule out reparameterization.

item.title: 6. RL Fundamentals II
item.itunes:title: RL Fundamentals II
item.description: Actor-critic: a learned critic V estimates advantages. TD learning bootstraps with delta equal to r plus gamma V of next state minus V of state. Monte Carlo is unbiased but high variance, TD is low variance but biased, n-step and lambda-returns interpolate. GAE: advantage equals the sum of gamma lambda to the l times delta at t plus l. Lambda 0 is one-step TD, lambda 1 is Monte Carlo return minus V. Compute with one backward recursion, no bootstrapping past terminal states. Critic target equals advantage plus V. LLM RLHF PPO: per-token reward is minus beta times the log ratio to the reference, plus the reward model score at the last token, typically gamma 1. Initialize the critic from the RM, warm it up, track explained variance. Importance sampling reweights by p over q. Trajectory-level ratios explode over long sequences, so use per-token ratios and stay close to the behavior policy.

item.title: 7. Learning from Human Preferences
item.itunes:title: Learning from Human Preferences
item.description: Good behavior is easier to recognize than to specify; pairwise comparisons cancel per-labeler offsets and beat absolute ratings for fuzzy quality. Bradley Terry: probability A preferred equals sigmoid of r(A) minus r(B). Loss is negative log sigmoid of chosen minus rejected; gradient weight is one minus sigmoid of the gap, so noisy labels get the biggest gradients. Rewards are defined only up to a constant: normalize. Christiano 2017: three asynchronous loops, ensembles, a random-response noise floor, online reward model training; offline reward models get exploited, and humans themselves can be fooled. KL-regularized objective: maximize reward minus beta times KL to a reference. Optimal policy is the reference reweighted by exp of reward over beta, the seed of DPO. Adaptive KL controllers target a KL value.

item.title: 8. InstructGPT and the ChatGPT Moment
item.itunes:title: InstructGPT and the ChatGPT Moment
item.description: Recipe: SFT on demonstrations, reward model on ranked comparisons, PPO with per-token KL to the SFT model, iterated. About 13k SFT prompts, 33k RM prompts, 31k PPO prompts; about 40 screened contractors. Details: split by user ID; SFT overfits validation loss after about 1 epoch but more epochs improve sample quality, so select checkpoints by RM score; 6B RM; rankings of K from 4 to 9 give K choose 2 pairs, all batched as one element, one epoch; RM bias set so demonstrations average zero; value initialized from RM. Alignment tax: regressions on SQuAD, DROP, HellaSwag, WMT French to English. PPO-ptx mixes pretraining log-likelihood into the loss and works better than raising the KL coefficient. B InstructGPT preferred over 175B GPT-3; 175B InstructGPT preferred over GPT-3 about 85 percent of the time. Alignment and capability are separate axes, and RLHF compute is tiny next to pretraining.

item.title: 9. Supervised Fine-Tuning, Done Right
item.itunes:title: Supervised Fine-Tuning, Done Right
item.description: The chat template is part of the model: special tokens with trainable embeddings, one render function for train/eval/serve, token-level round-trip tests. Mask prompt, system and tool-output tokens; train on every assistant turn including end-of-turn; choose token vs sequence loss averaging deliberately and normalize correctly across gradient accumulation. Pack with block-diagonal attention (varlen kernels) and reset position IDs per example. Select checkpoints on generation-based evals, not validation loss (InstructGPT, LIMA).

item.title: 10. Reward Models and Their Discontents
item.itunes:title: Reward Models and Their Discontents
item.description: RM = LM backbone + scalar head read at the true final token; init from SFT; ~1 epoch; group all K-choose-2 pairs per prompt in one batch element. BT loss: -log sigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected); only differences matter, so center/normalize rewards. Accuracy ceiling ~ inter-annotator agreement. Margins (Llama 2), multi-attribute heads (HelpSteer), separate helpful/safety RMs; normalize, gate, and log each reward component. Overoptimization (Gao et al.): gold reward vs d = sqrt(KL) is d(alpha - beta d) for best-of-n and d(alpha - beta log d) for RL; bigger RMs delay the peak; best-of-n KL <= log n - (n-1)/n (an upper bound, Beirami et al.; ~1.8 nats at n=16).

item.title: 11. Direct Preference Optimization and Friends
item.itunes:title: Direct Preference Optimization and Friends
item.description: KL-regularized RLHF has a closed-form optimum: pi* is proportional to pi_ref times exp(r over beta); invert it so reward is beta times log(pi over pi_ref) plus a prompt-only term. Plug into Bradley-Terry: the partition function cancels and DPO is a logistic loss on beta times the difference of chosen and rejected log-ratios. No reward model, no sampling; reference log-probs can be precomputed. The DPO gradient upweights pairs the implicit reward ranks wrongly; beta is still a KL strength (smaller beta lets the policy move further). Failure modes: chosen log-prob falls (likelihood displacement), length exploitation, margins blow up on deterministic preferences. Watch chosen/rejected log-probs separately, length, sampled KL, and generative evals.

item.title: 12. PPO for LLMs in the Trenches
item.itunes:title: PPO for LLMs in the Trenches
item.description: Token-level MDP: state = prompt + tokens so far, action = next token, deterministic transitions, gamma 1, RM score on the last real token, per-token KL penalty (k1) in the reward. Value head = linear layer on the final hidden state per position; separate critic usually initialized from the RM; consider critic warmup and lambda 1 for value targets on long responses (VC-PPO). One iteration: rollout -> old log-probs, ref log-probs, values, RM score -> per-token rewards -> GAE backward -> whiten advantages over valid tokens -> a few PPO epochs of clipped policy loss + clipped value loss. KL estimators (samples from pi, r = pi_ref/pi): k1 = -log r (unbiased, noisy, can be negative; zero expected gradient as a loss); k2 = 0.5 (log r)^2 (biased; as a loss gives the reverse-KL gradient); k3 = (r - 1) - log r (unbiased, nonnegative, low variance; as a loss gives the forward-KL gradient).

item.title: 18. Agents and Multi-Turn RL
item.itunes:title: Agents and Multi-Turn RL
item.description: An agent is an LM policy in a loop with a real, partially observable environment; the scaffold (agent-computer interface) is part of the policy, so train on what you ship. Loss and KL go only over tokens the policy sampled; mask prompts and tool observations, and unit-test the mask. Token-in, token-out: never re-tokenize history; store exact token IDs, the mask, and per-token sampler log-probs. Default credit assignment: trajectory-level outcome reward with a group baseline (GRPO/RLOO style); filter tasks to the learnable pass-rate band. Critics, turn-level methods (ArCHer), and shaping each have costs; only potential-based shaping preserves the optimal policy.

item.title: 19. Reward Hacking and Specification Gaming
item.itunes:title: Reward Hacking and Specification Gaming
item.description: Assume every reward is hackable (Skalse et al.); more capable optimizers find more hacks (Pan et al.). Build a system that detects and closes holes. Coding-hack taxonomy: attack the tests, special-case the tests, attack the runner (early exit, skip, conftest patching), attack the comparison (always-equal objects, mocks), attack the environment (reference solutions, git history, network), attack the measurement (timers, caches). Layered grader defenses: hidden and randomized tests, protected files restored at grading, grading in a fresh container from the diff only, structured per-test results instead of exit codes, skipped counts as failed, hardened sandbox. Learned rewards and judges get hacked via length, formatting, flattery, persuasion; sycophancy is the product-facing form. Every new reward signal needs an eval for its likely failure mode.

item.title: 20. RL Infrastructure at Scale
item.itunes:title: RL Infrastructure at Scale
item.description: Generation dominates RL cost: decode is autoregressive and memory-bandwidth bound; KV cache size (about 128 KB per token for a 32-layer, 8-KV-head, 128-dim bf16 model) caps the decode batch. PagedAttention, prefix caching for GRPO groups and multi-turn agents, and continuous batching are core RL infrastructure. Colocated vs disaggregated; synchronous vs asynchronous. Async trades staleness for wall-clock speed; bound staleness and correct with importance ratios. Weight sync: reshard, bucketed NCCL broadcast, re-fuse; verify every sync with a probe-sequence log-prob check.

item.title: 24. Evals, Diagnostics, and Putting It All Together
item.itunes:title: Evals, Diagnostics, and Putting It All Together
item.description: An eval is a statistical estimate: SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n); 500 items at 50% gives about +/-4.4 points 95% CI; HumanEval (164) about 3.9-point SE. MDE for a paired comparison (alpha 0.05, power 0.8) is about 2.8 x SE of the difference; multiple comparisons across many evals; checkpoint-selection bias (select on one split, report on another). Validate programmatic graders too: mutation-style known-wrong solutions, flaky-test reruns, regrading to measure environment variance. Use paired per-question differences, clustered SEs, multiple samples per item, multiple training seeds; compute minimum detectable effect first.
